title: Building the oracle, stage by stage
intro: The parent named the four stages in order. This level walks each one at working resolution: what the reconstructor's loss actually measures, how five million sampled continuations become a 3.4-million-entry dictionary, what the matching-pursuit teacher does step by step, what the reinforcement stage adds that the teacher could not, and what the 31% figure is a fraction of.

chapters.title: A model trained backwards
chapters.body:
A language model maps an activation to the text that follows it. The [[reconstructor-model]], the first stage of [[oracle-training]], is trained to run that map the other way: given a phrase, it produces the [[residual-stream]] activation that would sit at the position immediately before it.

The choice of target is not arbitrary. A [[template-lens]] template for a word is the mean activation over passages written so that the word is the natural continuation, then centered and whitened, and the result is used for readout and steering in the same way as a [[j-lens-vector]]. [[template-construction]] costs a few hundred forward passes per word, and every word has to be named in advance.

The reconstructor amortizes that procedure. One fine-tuned copy of the subject model, run once, stands in for the whole averaging pipeline, and it accepts phrases nobody enumerated.

The loss repays unpacking. Raw [[activations]] in the residual stream do not vary equally in every direction; a few directions carry very large variance, and an ordinary cosine distance between two activations is dominated by them. Whitening removes that imbalance. The prediction and the target are each multiplied by $\Sigma^{-1/2}$, where $\Sigma$ is the residual stream's covariance, then scaled to unit length, and the loss is the mean squared error between the two vectors. That is the same metric the template lens already works in, and it is equivalent to cosine error there.

One consequence runs through everything downstream. The teacher's decompositions, the reinforcement-learning reward and the headline reconstruction number are all computed in this whitened space rather than in raw activation space.

Phrase length is drawn uniformly from one to thirty-two tokens, so a single model has to cover both a two-token fragment and a full sentence, with every length weighted equally in training.

chapters.title: Five million continuations, minus the repeats
chapters.body:
The dictionary is harvested, not learned. A [[sparse-autoencoder]] finds its dictionary directions by optimizing against the activations themselves. Here the entries are just text the model already wrote, pushed through the reconstructor one phrase at a time.

The arithmetic is worth walking. Roughly one million start positions are sampled from a held-out corpus of [[assistant-persona]]-turn text, the model's own side of a conversation and the distribution [[post-training]] shapes. At each position five continuations are taken, of 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 tokens, which is five million phrases before any filtering. Deduplication within each length brings that to roughly 3.4 million. About a third of the sampled phrases are therefore repeats of one another.

The lengths are counted in tokenizer units rather than words, so a 2-token entry may be half a word or two short ones [[tokenizer-vocabulary]].

The paper does not break the 3.4 million down by length. Short continuations repeat far more often than long ones, since two-token strings of common words recur constantly while a specific thirty-two-token stretch rarely does, so the surviving entries are presumably concentrated at the longer lengths. That is an inference from how deduplication works, not a reported figure.

What the dictionary is for constrains what its gaps cost. It is the teacher's search space, and only the teacher's. Any phrase that never appeared in the sampled corpus has no entry, so the teacher cannot select it, and the labels the oracle learns from are bounded by what assistant text happened to say. This is the limit the later reinforcement stage is meant to escape, and it is the reason [[multi-token-lens-extensions]] of this kind are not simply a longer vocabulary bolted onto the [[single-token-limitation]].

chapters.title: A search procedure stands in for labels
chapters.body:
There are no ground-truth phrase lists for an activation, so the teacher computes them by search.

Non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit proceeds greedily. The whitened activation starts as the residual. Every candidate direction in the dictionary is scored by its inner product with that residual, negative scores are discarded, and the highest-scoring phrase joins the selected set. The coefficients of all selected phrases are then refit jointly by non-negative least squares, which is the orthogonal step: the new residual is made orthogonal to the span of everything chosen so far, not merely to the latest pick. The residual is recomputed and the loop runs again, up to sixteen phrases.

For each activation the teacher records the ordered list, the fitted coefficients, and the fraction of whitened variance explained.

This is the same greedy family as [[gradient-pursuit]], the algorithm the paper uses for [[sparse-decomposition]] of activations over [[j-space]] directions. Only the dictionary differs: J-lens vectors there, reconstructor outputs here.

Non-negativity is not incidental. A coefficient cannot go below zero, so a phrase can be present or absent but never subtracted from the reconstruction, which matches reading an activation as a sum of active features under the [[linear-representation-hypothesis]] and its [[superposition]] and [[sparse-frame]] framing.

The decomposition runs at one phrase length at a time, because the oracle is later queried at a fixed length and needs a target list for each.

The random-half restriction does a specific job. On each datapoint the search may use only half the entries at that length, drawn at random, so the same activation decomposed twice yields different lists. A student that learned one fixed ranking over the dictionary and printed it regardless of input would score badly against those labels. It has to condition on the injected activation instead, much as dropout forces a network off any single fixed path.

chapters.title: Imitation first, reward second
chapters.body:
The oracle receives its activation as a vector written directly into its own residual stream, not as text, while the prompt states the requested phrase length $N$ and count $K$ in words. The appendix does not say at which layer or position the injection happens.

The supervised stage is compression. The teacher reached its list by sixteen rounds of scoring and refitting over hundreds of thousands of candidates; the oracle has to emit the first $K$ of those phrases in one left-to-right generation. Decoding a single activation therefore costs a sampled generation from a fine-tuned model, where a [[j-lens-readout]] costs one matrix multiply.

Reinforcement learning then runs on fresh assistant-turn activations, and the reward is arithmetic rather than preference-based: the fraction of whitened variance the generated phrases reconstruct, with small penalties for missing the requested count and length. Nothing resembling a human preference model appears, unlike [[rlhf]]. Because the penalties are small, $N$ and $K$ function as strong requests rather than hard constraints.

The reward is the inference-time objective itself, and that is what lets the [[oracle-lens]] leave its dictionary behind. The teacher could only ever select entries that existed in the harvested set. The reward scores whatever the oracle writes, so a phrase never sampled into the dictionary can still earn credit if its reconstructed direction helps explain the activation. The dictionary trains the oracle without bounding what it may say about a [[verbalizable-representation]].

How much the reinforcement stage contributes is not quantified here. The paper reports one reconstruction figure, for the RL-refined checkpoint, with no supervised-only number beside it, and the readouts in [[fig-64]] likewise come from an RL-refined checkpoint.

chapters.title: Thirty-one percent, and what is held frozen
chapters.body:
At inference the oracle's phrases carry no weights. It emits text, and nothing in that text states how much of each phrase is present in the activation. So each sampled phrase is mapped back to a direction by the frozen reconstructor, and the coefficients over just those $K$ directions are recovered by a non-negative least-squares refit against the original activation. Non-negativity keeps the reconstruction inside the same cone geometry the paper uses for the workspace [[union-of-cones]].

The headline number needs its units read carefully. The refined oracle explains on average 31% of the whitened activation variance, across assistant-turn positions of a held-out corpus of on-policy transcripts, meaning transcripts the subject model generated itself rather than text written by someone else. The whitening introduced in the first stage is still in force, so this is not 31% of raw activation variance.

The comparison the paper draws is with the [[natural-language-autoencoder]], which also pairs a verbalizer with a reconstructor. There the reconstructor is trained in tandem with the verbalizer, and the paper names the risk that follows: the pair can settle into a private code, where the verbalizer emits text that is ungrounded and the reconstructor adapts to make use of it anyway. In the oracle lens the reconstructor is trained in advance against a specified target, held frozen through reinforcement learning, and the reconstruction is restricted to a linear combination of its template vectors.

The claim drawn from that is hedged, and the hedge should be kept: the authors suspect the oracle lens is less likely to confabulate. No experiment separating grounded from confabulated phrases is reported.

The cost is stated plainly. Natural-language autoencoders reach considerably higher reconstruction accuracy. One interpretation the paper offers, without testing it, is that the oracle recovers only what is in the workspace while an autoencoder attempts the entire vector. The workspace's own variance figures sit nearby but are not directly comparable, being measured over J-lens directions and against a random control [[j-space-capacity]] [[excess-variance-explained]] [[j-space-occupancy]].
